title: The Spell code review checklist targets deception patterns, not only vulnerabilities
content:
A.1.10.2.4.12.3.1.9 asks validators to look for "low-level assembly operations," opcodes such as "`delegatecall`, `callcode`, or `selfdestruct`," "suspicious-looking payments or transfers," and "any other malicious or unauthorized code," including "cross-checking the Solidity code in `actions()` against the Executive Sheet and the Executive Document. Each action must be authorized per the Atlas."

A.1.10.2.4.12.3.3.10 extends the list into territory most audit checklists omit: "Hidden state changes: Look for retrieval functions (e.g., `get` or `view`) that include assignments (`=`)"; "External Calls At The End" as a reentrancy signal; "Force Ether, DAI or SKY Reception: Look for a `receive` function with no logic"; "Use of `tx.origin`" instead of `msg.sender`; and "**Function Naming Overlaps**: A contract might have function names that are similar or overlap with common Solidity functions to mislead a reviewer. Check for misleading function names (e.g., `transfer`, `approve`, `mint`) with unexpected logic."

The last two entries are not vulnerability classes — they are *social engineering embedded in source code*. A function named `transfer` that does something else, or a getter that quietly mutates state, exploits the reviewer's pattern-matching rather than the EVM. A reader skimming for familiar shapes sees what they expect.

This matters because Spell review is performed under time pressure by people reading a lot of similar-looking code, which is exactly the condition in which name-based shortcuts substitute for reading. Naming the technique makes the shortcut itself the thing to check.

The threat model on display is an insider who knows the process: not someone hoping a bug is missed, but someone crafting code that *reads* correct to a competent reviewer following the checklist.
description: Alongside delegatecall and selfdestruct, validators are told to look for view functions that assign state, misleading function names, and receive() with no logic — code written to fool a reviewer.
